recorded.outcome:q-two-services: Option c. Section 'Pattern Letters Are Case-Sensitive, and YYYY Is the Year of the Week': 'US weeks start on Sunday, and the week holding 1 January belongs to the new year, so from Sunday 28 December 2025 it prints 2026. UK weeks follow ISO-8601: they start on Monday and belong to the year holding at least four of their days.' The output shows the same calendar case (1 Jan 2026 is also a Thursday): '2025-12-28   YYYY en-US: 2026-12-28   YYYY en-GB: 2025-12-28'. Under the UK rule, Sunday 28 Dec 2031 closes the Mon 22 to Sun 28 Dec week, which has all its days in 2031, so en-GB prints 2031-12-28 and en-US prints 2032-12-28.

recorded.outcome:q-signup-form: Option c. Section 'ofPattern Turns 30 February Into the 28th Unless the Resolver Is STRICT, and STRICT Needs uuuu': 'STRICT with `yyyy` and no `G` refuses every date: a year-of-era means nothing without an era (AD or BC), and STRICT won't assume one. Use `uuuu`, which needs no era.' The output shows even a valid date refused: 'yyyy-MM-dd, STRICT  2026-02-28 -> ... Unable to obtain LocalDate from TemporalAccessor: {MonthOfYear=2, DayOfMonth=28, YearOfEra=2026}'. The quiz uses dd/MM/yyyy, but the page's 'every date' covers it.

recorded.outcome:q-ingest-column: Option b. Section 'An Offset in the Text Is Part of the Value, So Parse Into a Type That Keeps It': '`LocalDateTime` has no field for the offset, so the parse dropped it without an error. Stored as UTC, every event from the `+01:00` sender lands an hour late.' Output: '2026-03-14T10:30:00+01:00 / as LocalDateTime:  2026-03-14T10:30'. The local time is kept and the offset dropped, so 09:30 is stored.
